What an Advisor Does for an AI Company

Strategy · AI

In short: An advisor helps an AI company decide, introduces it to the people who matter, and tells it which advantages will not last. Scope the relationship in writing, vest the equity, and hire separately for anything that is a job.

Key points

  • An advisor offers pattern recognition in exchange for a small amount of equity, a modest fee, or both, and does not run a function.
  • The most valuable advisors introduce buyers, partners and practitioners; in AI one credible introduction can beat a year of outbound.
  • Good advisors say which parts of the plan survive the next model release, and translate model capabilities into buyer outcomes.
  • Structure it with a written scope, vesting with a cliff, a named founder owner and a six-month review.
  • Do not ask advisors to run marketing, manage vendors, write the deck, close deals or be on call.

AI companies accumulate advisors faster than almost any other kind of startup. The category is new, the founders are often technical, investors ask who is around the table, and a well-known name on the deck is cheap to add.

Most of those relationships produce a logo and a quarterly call. A few produce decisions the company would not otherwise have made. The difference is in what the advisor is asked to do.

What an advisor is

An advisor is a person with relevant experience who helps the founders make better decisions, in exchange for a small amount of equity, a modest fee, or both. The advisor does not run a function, does not do the work, and is not accountable for results. What they offer is pattern recognition: they have seen this decision before, in a company like this, and they know how it tends to go.

That is valuable in AI precisely because so few people have seen the current decisions before. But it also defines the limits.

What a good advisor contributes to an AI company

Customer and buyer access. The most valuable advisors introduce the company to the buyers, partners, and practitioners who will decide whether it exists in two years. In AI, where trust is the product, one credible introduction can be worth more than a year of outbound.

A view on what is durable. Founders close to the technology overestimate how long a capability advantage lasts. An advisor who has watched several model cycles can say which parts of the plan survive the next release and which do not, and push the company toward the workflow, the data, and the distribution that persist.

Commercial translation. Technical founders describe what the model does. Buyers want to know what changes for them. An advisor who has sold into the relevant industry can turn the first into the second, and can tell the company which claims will get it thrown out of a procurement process.

Regulatory and reputational judgment. What may be claimed about accuracy and safety, which use cases attract scrutiny, how a data-handling decision will read in eighteen months. This is where an advisor's caution earns its equity.

Distribution realism. Which channels will carry an AI product to its buyer, what that costs, and why the crowded AI advertising auction is the wrong place to start. This is the advice we most often find missing.

How the relationship should be structured

A written scope: the topics the advisor covers, the cadence, and the introductions they will attempt. A vesting schedule on any equity, with a cliff, so an advisor who disappears does not keep the grant. A named founder who owns the relationship and prepares for each session with specific decisions rather than an update. A review at six months.

What an advisor should not be asked to do

Run marketing. Manage vendors. Write the deck. Close the deal. Be on call. Each of these is a job, and an advisor who takes it on becomes an underpaid, unaccountable employee, which is bad for both sides. When the company needs those things, it should hire them, from a fractional leader, an agency, or a full-time person.

The strongest advisor relationships are narrow, structured, and used for decisions. The weakest are broad, casual, and used for reassurance.

lowob takeaway: An advisor helps an AI company decide, introduces it to the people who matter, and tells it which advantages will not last. Scope the relationship in writing, vest the equity, and hire separately for anything that is a job.

Common questions

What does an advisor do for an AI startup?

Helps the founders make better decisions through pattern recognition: buyer and partner introductions, a view on which advantages are durable, commercial translation, regulatory and reputational judgment, and distribution realism.

How should an advisor relationship be structured?

With a written scope covering topics, cadence and introductions, a vesting schedule with a cliff on any equity, a named founder who owns the relationship and brings specific decisions, and a review at six months.

What should you not ask a startup advisor to do?

Run marketing, manage vendors, write the deck, close the deal or be on call. Each is a job, and an advisor who takes it on becomes an underpaid, unaccountable employee.
